overview.title: Why reuse only the convolutional base (Figure 8.12)
overview.subsection: 8.3.1 Feature extraction with a pretrained model
overview.main_topic: Feature extraction as swapping the classifier on a frozen pretrained convolutional base; why the dense classifier is generally not reused (class-specific, no spatial information); how layer depth determines how generic features are
overview.central_idea: For convnets, feature extraction means running new data through a previously trained convolutional base, kept frozen, and training a new, randomly initialized classifier on its output. The base is reused because its feature maps are generic presence maps of visual concepts that keep spatial information. The original classifier encodes only the original classes and discards location. Earlier layers are more generic than deeper ones, so for very different datasets you may reuse only the first few layers.
overview.importance: These are the design principles behind transfer learning in vision: what to keep, what to discard, and how deep to cut. They apply well beyond this chapter, for example to the object detection and segmentation backbones used later in the book.

summary:
The page finishes the definition begun on p.280. For convnets, **feature extraction** means taking the **convolutional base** of a previously trained network, running the new data through it, and training a new classifier on top of its output.

**Figure 8.12** shows this in three panels. On the left is the original network: input, trained convolutional base, trained classifier, prediction. In the middle, the trained classifier is **crossed out**. On the right, a **new classifier (randomly initialized)** sits on top of the **trained convolutional base (frozen)**. Arrows between the panels show that the same base is carried across.

The authors then answer **why only the base is reused**. Reusing the classifier "should be avoided" in general, for two reasons:

1. **Generality.** Convolutional feature maps are "presence maps of generic concepts over a picture", useful for any vision problem. Classifier representations are specific to the original class set and encode only the probability that each class is present in the whole picture.
2. **Spatial information.** Densely connected layers "get rid of the notion of space". Convolutional feature maps still describe where objects are, so for problems where location matters, dense features are "largely useless".

A final refinement: generality also **depends on depth within the base**. Early layers extract local, highly generic features (edges, colors, textures). Higher layers extract abstract concepts such as "cat ear" or "dog eye". So if your new dataset differs a lot from the original training data, you may be better off using only the first few layers of the model (the sentence finishes on p.282). The next page adds that, for dogs vs. cats, reusing ImageNet's dense layers could actually help, but the authors deliberately skip it to cover the general case.

paragraphs.what_it_says: For convnets, feature extraction means taking a previously trained network's convolutional base, running new data through it, and training a new classifier on its output (Figure 8.12).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The pretrained base becomes a fixed preprocessing function that turns each image into a feature tensor. Only the small new classifier learns from your labeled data. In Figure 8.12 the base is marked "(frozen)" and the new head "(randomly initialized)".
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the operational recipe implemented in the following listings with Xception from KerasHub (p.282). It also explains the two implementation choices on p.283: precompute the base's outputs once, or run the frozen base inside the model so that augmentation can be used.

paragraphs.excerpt: Why only reuse the convolutional base? Could you reuse the densely connected classifier as well?
paragraphs.what_it_says: Reusing the dense classifier should generally be avoided. The convolutional base learns generic, reusable representations (presence maps of generic concepts over a picture). The classifier's representations are specific to the original classes and say only how likely each class is in the whole picture. Dense layers also discard spatial information, which convolutional feature maps keep, so dense features are largely useless when object location matters.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A convolutional feature map of shape (H, W, C) answers, for each of C learned patterns, "how strongly is this pattern present at each location?" That is useful whatever you are trying to classify. A Dense layer collapses the spatial grid into a single vector tuned to separating the original 1,000 ImageNet classes. Its outputs are tied to those classes and no longer say *where* anything is.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This tells you where to cut a pretrained network. It is also why later tasks that need location, such as object detection and image segmentation, build on convolutional backbones rather than classifier outputs.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Flattening or global pooling followed by Dense layers removes the spatial index. After global average pooling, a (7, 7, C) map becomes a C-vector with no record of position.

terminology.meaning: A feature map whose value at each position measures how strongly a particular learned pattern appears there.

paragraphs.what_it_says: How generic a convolution layer's representations are depends on its depth. Early layers extract local, highly generic feature maps (edges, colors, textures), and higher layers extract abstract concepts ("cat ear", "dog eye"). If your new dataset differs a lot from the original one, you may be better off using only the first few layers (the sentence continues on p.282).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Specificity increases gradually with depth, not only at the base/classifier boundary. Deep layers of an ImageNet model are tuned to ImageNet-like objects. For a very different domain, those abstract features may not apply, while low-level edges and textures still do.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This gives you a dial for transfer learning: how much of the pretrained network to keep. A distant target domain calls for a shallower cut, and a close one, like dogs vs. cats on ImageNet, can use the full base.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: in practice you can cut the base at an intermediate layer by building a model whose output is that layer's activation, then train a classifier on those earlier feature maps.

concepts.name: Feature extraction (convnet version)
concepts.definition: Keeping a pretrained convolutional base frozen, running new data through it, and training a new randomly initialized classifier on its outputs.
concepts.intuition: Keep the eyes, replace the decision maker.
concepts.technical: $\hat y = g_\phi(f_\theta(x))$ with the pretrained $\theta$ frozen and only $\phi$ learned (Figure 8.12, right panel).
concepts.significance: It is the core transfer-learning recipe of section 8.3.1.
concepts.example: Xception's base followed by a new Dense sigmoid classifier for dogs vs. cats.
concepts.misconception: The old classifier is not kept and extended. It is discarded (crossed out in Figure 8.12).

concepts.name: Convolutional base
concepts.definition: The conv/pool part of a trained convnet, whose feature maps are generic, spatial presence maps of visual concepts.
concepts.intuition: A bank of pattern detectors that reports what appears where.
concepts.technical: Its output is a tensor of shape (H, W, C) that preserves location, unlike Dense layer outputs.
concepts.significance: It is the reusable part of a pretrained network.
concepts.misconception: Not all of its layers are equally generic. Deeper layers are more task-specific.

concepts.name: Depth vs. generality of features
concepts.definition: Earlier convnet layers learn local, generic features, and later layers learn more abstract, task-specific ones.
concepts.intuition: Letters, then words, then topic-specific jargon.
concepts.technical: Early layers learn edges, colors and textures. Higher layers learn object parts such as "cat ear" or "dog eye".
concepts.significance: It determines how deep to cut a pretrained model for a new domain.
concepts.example: For very different data, such as satellite or medical images, reuse only the first few layers.
concepts.misconception: Using more pretrained layers is not always better. If the domains differ, deep features can be poorly matched to the new task.

concepts.name: Loss of spatial information in dense layers
concepts.definition: Densely connected layers remove the notion of space, while convolutional feature maps keep object location.
concepts.intuition: A dense layer gives a verdict without saying where it saw the evidence.
concepts.technical: Flatten or global pooling followed by Dense mixes all positions into one vector.
concepts.significance: Dense features are "largely useless" when location matters.
concepts.example: Detecting where a dog is in an image needs feature maps, not class probabilities.
concepts.misconception: Class probabilities are not a compact substitute for features. They throw away both genericity and location.

deeper.title: Reading Figure 8.12 panel by panel
deeper.body:
- **Left:** the original pretrained model. Input goes through the *trained convolutional base*, then the *trained classifier*, then a prediction.
- **Middle:** the same base, with the *trained classifier crossed out*, so it is removed.
- **Right:** the *trained convolutional base (frozen)* with a *new classifier (randomly initialized)* on top, producing predictions for the new task.

The horizontal arrows between the bases show that it is the same base throughout. Only the head changes.

deeper.title: Choosing where to cut
deeper.body:
1. **Similar domain and classes** (dogs vs. cats with ImageNet): reuse the whole base. Per p.282, even the dense layers could help, but the book skips them to show the general case.
2. **Same kind of images, different classes** (furniture, p.280): reuse the whole base and train a new classifier.
3. **Very different domain:** reuse only the first few layers, whose edges, colors and textures still transfer, and train the rest.
4. **Location matters** (detection, segmentation): never rely on dense-layer features. Use the convolutional feature maps.

deeper.title: Analogy: a newspaper's reporters and editor
deeper.body: The reporters (the convolutional base) gather detailed, location-tagged facts: what happened, and where. The editor (the classifier) condenses them into a headline for one particular readership. A different newspaper can reuse the reporters' notes but needs its own editor, because the old headlines answer the old readership's questions and no longer say where events took place.

misconceptions.claim: Reusing the whole pretrained model, classifier included, is always best.
misconceptions.correction: In general the classifier should not be reused. Its representations are specific to the original classes and contain no spatial information.

misconceptions.claim: All layers of the convolutional base are equally generic.
misconceptions.correction: Generality decreases with depth. Early layers are highly generic, and higher layers encode abstract, dataset-specific concepts.

misconceptions.claim: Dense features are fine for localization tasks.
misconceptions.correction: Dense layers "get rid of the notion of space", so for location-dependent problems they are largely useless.

misconceptions.claim: In feature extraction, the base is updated together with the new classifier.
misconceptions.correction: Figure 8.12 marks the base "(frozen)". Updating it is fine-tuning (section 8.3.2, p.288).

takeaways: Convnet feature extraction means a frozen pretrained convolutional base plus a new, randomly initialized classifier (Figure 8.12).
Reuse the base, not the classifier. Base features are generic presence maps, while classifier outputs are specific to the original classes.
Dense layers discard spatial information. Convolutional feature maps keep object location.
Feature generality decreases with depth: edges, colors and textures early, "cat ear" and "dog eye" later.
For a very different dataset, reuse only the first few layers of the base.

options: Base frozen (pretrained), classifier new and randomly initialized
questions.answer: Base frozen (pretrained), classifier new and randomly initialized
questions.explanation: The labels read "Trained convolutional base (frozen)" and "New classifier (randomly initialized)". The other combinations describe fine-tuning, inference only, or training from scratch.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the authors give for not reusing the densely connected classifier.
questions.answer: (1) Its representations are specific to the original classes and encode only per-class presence probabilities for the whole picture. (2) Dense layers discard spatial information about where objects are.
questions.explanation: Both reasons are stated in the main paragraph. The convolutional feature maps, by contrast, are generic and spatial.

questions.question: What does it mean that a convnet's feature maps are "presence maps of generic concepts over a picture"?
questions.answer: Each channel of a feature map indicates, at each spatial location, how strongly a learned pattern (an edge, texture or part) is present. That information is useful for many vision tasks, not just the original classes.
questions.explanation: This is the authors' justification for reusing the base. The phrase combines genericity (the concepts) with spatial structure (over a picture).

questions.question: You want to classify microscope images of cells using an ImageNet-pretrained convnet. Following this page's advice, what should you consider?
options: Reusing the entire network including the ImageNet classifier
Using only the first few layers of the convolutional base for feature extraction
Using only the deepest layers, because they are the most abstract
questions.answer: Using only the first few layers of the convolutional base for feature extraction
questions.explanation: When the new dataset differs a lot from the original, early generic layers (edges, colors, textures) transfer better than deep abstract ones such as "cat ear". The ImageNet classifier is class-specific. The page does not advise abandoning pretraining.

questions.question: Why are densely connected features "largely useless" for problems where object location matters?
questions.answer: Dense layers mix all spatial positions into a single vector and so remove the notion of space. Convolutional feature maps still record where patterns occur.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly on the page, and it is why location-sensitive tasks rely on convolutional backbones.
